extraction.name: SWE-Gym
extraction.description: An environment for training software engineering agents containing 2,438 real-world Python task instances with codebases, executable runtime environments, unit tests, and natural-language task descriptions.
extraction.creator: Jiayi Pan; Xingyao Wang; Graham Neubig; Navdeep Jaitly; Heng Ji; Alane Suhr; Yizhe Zhang
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was constructed by filtering GitHub repositories, extracting task instances from GitHub issues and pull requests using the SWE-Bench extraction script, associating instances with versions, semi-automatically collecting version information, manually configuring dependencies for executable environments, and validating instances with execution-based scripts before filtering failed instances.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Software Collection, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real-world software engineering tasks sourced from pull requests and GitHub issues in Python repositories, including issue descriptions, repository snapshots, unit tests, code, and solutions.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Instances were versioned, executable environments were set up with pre-installed dependencies, gold patches were validated with execution-based scripts, and failed instances were filtered out. SWE-Gym Lite further excludes tasks editing more than one file, poorly described tasks, tasks with complex diffs, and tests focused on error messages.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human annotation was used to manually configure dependencies for task instances and create executable environments; annotations were done by a subset of the authors.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Instances were validated by checking that the gold patch passes more unit tests than the original code, and failed instances were filtered out.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper discusses that improved automated software engineering could increase developer productivity and accessibility, may affect software engineering jobs and issues of code ownership, licensing, and attribution, and could be misused to automate malicious code creation; it calls for responsible deployment considering security, safety, and economic impacts.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset has a long-tail task distribution across repositories, with pandas comprising nearly one-third of tasks and bokeh about one percent; the authors also note that ignoring executable environments could introduce distribution bias.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited in environment diversity, including the number of repositories, types of tasks, and programming languages. The paper also notes that SWE-Gym Raw lacks executable environments and guarantees about unit test effectiveness.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training software engineering agents and verifiers; rapid prototyping with SWE-Gym Lite; supporting future research in SWE agent development and automatic dataset synthesis.

name.evidence: We present SWE-Gym, the first environment for training software engineering (SWE) agents.

description.evidence: SWE-Gym contains 2,438 real-world task instances, each comprising a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language.

inLanguage.evidence: SWE-Gym contains 2,438 real-world task instances, each comprising a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We first use SEART GitHub search to filter a list of initial repositories. We use SWE-Bench’s instance extraction script to convert these repositories into task instances, each corresponding to a GitHub issue including the natural language description of the issue, a snapshot of the repository in which the issue was created, and a set of unit tests. We generalize SWE-Bench’s versioning script to support versioning via script execution, and semi-automatically collect versions for each instance based on information available in the repository (e.g., pyproject.toml, git tag, etc). To address this, we manually configure dependencies for each task instance using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. We then use SWE-Bench’s execution-based validation script to ensure that the gold patch (the human-submitted code diff) passes more unit tests than the original code. After validation and filtering out failed instances, we obtained 2,438 unit-test-validated instances from 11 repositories.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: SWE-Gym comprises 2,438 real-world software engineering tasks sourced from pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories, with pre-configured executable environments and expert-validated test cases, constructed in close alignment with SWE-Bench (Jimenez et al., 2024). We use SWE-Bench’s instance extraction script to convert these repositories into task instances, each corresponding to a GitHub issue including the natural language description of the issue, a snapshot of the repository in which the issue was created, and a set of unit tests. While SWE-Gym Raw instances contain code, issue descriptions, and the solution, they do not contain executable environments or a guarantee that its unit tests are effective in evaluating the correctness of a solution.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: we select Python repositories that were created before July 1, 2022

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: We generalize SWE-Bench’s versioning script to support versioning via script execution, and semi-automatically collect versions for each instance based on information available in the repository (e.g., pyproject.toml, git tag, etc). To address this, we manually configure dependencies for each task instance using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. We then use SWE-Bench’s execution-based validation script to ensure that the gold patch (the human-submitted code diff) passes more unit tests than the original code. After validation and filtering out failed instances, we obtained 2,438 unit-test-validated instances from 11 repositories. Similar to SWE-Bench Lite, this subset excludes tasks that require editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, those with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: To address this, we manually configure dependencies for each task instance using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. This process required approximately 200 human annotation hours. Annotations are done by a subset of the authors.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: We then use SWE-Bench’s execution-based validation script to ensure that the gold patch (the human-submitted code diff) passes more unit tests than the original code. After validation and filtering out failed instances, we obtained 2,438 unit-test-validated instances from 11 repositories.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: First, improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer’s productivity and accessibility across industries. Secondly, as these agents become more capable, they may impact software engineering jobs and require careful consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. Additionally, while we focus on legitimate software engineering tasks, similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code. We encourage future work to further explore frameworks for responsible deployment of software engineering agents, including considerations around security, safety, and economic impacts.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Fig. 2 illustrates that the task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattem. Notably, tasks associated with pandas comprise nearly one-third of the total, whereas tasks related to bokeh represent a mere one percent. Ignoring these environments could introduce distribution bias, diminishing SWE-Gym’s utility.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: SWE-Gym, while effective, is limited by its environment diversity, including the number of repositories, types of tasks, and programming languages. While SWE-Gym Raw instances contain code, issue descriptions, and the solution, they do not contain executable environments or a guarantee that its unit tests are effective in evaluating the correctness of a solution.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We present SWE-Gym, the first environment for training software engineering (SWE) agents. We use SWE-Gym to train language model based SWE agents. We use test suites included in SWE-Gym to determine whether sampled agent trajectories are successful or not. We also identify a subset of 230 tasks, SWE-Gym Lite, which contains generally easier and more self-contained tasks that are suitable for rapid prototyping. To support future research in SWE agent development and automatic dataset synthesis, we also release SWE-Gym Raw
